name: Ajanta Caves
overview:
The Ajanta Caves, in a horseshoe-shaped gorge of the Waghora River near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in Maharashtra, are about thirty rock-cut Buddhist caves famous for ancient wall paintings and sculpture. They were carved in two main phases. The first, from around the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE, is linked to the Satavahana period, and the second, in the 5th century CE, was supported by the Vakataka dynasty and its ministers. The caves were later abandoned, hidden by jungle, and rediscovered in 1819 by a British officer on a tiger hunt.

The beauty of Ajanta is its paintings. The murals, painted on plaster in natural pigments, illustrate the lives of the Buddha and the Jataka tales of his previous births, and show royal courts, travellers, women, animals and flowers with great elegance and emotion. The famous image of the Bodhisattva Padmapani in Cave 1 is widely regarded as a masterpiece of Indian painting. The sculpture is equally remarkable, including the large reclining Buddha in Cave 26 and the richly carved facade of the chaitya hall in Cave 19.

The caves include two types of structure. Chaitya halls were prayer halls with a stupa, such as Caves 9, 10, 19 and 26. Viharas were monasteries with cells for monks around a central hall, such as Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17. Their carving from solid basalt, with pillars, ceilings and details formed in the rock, is a remarkable engineering and artistic achievement.

Ajanta was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. It is famous as a high point of Buddhist art and as a window into daily life and belief in ancient India.

Visitors should note that lighting is limited to protect the paintings, and flash photography is not allowed. A visitor centre and replicas help explain the caves. It is a long day trip, about 100 km from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, and Ellora is a natural companion. Check current opening days and ticket rules with official sources.
